doc.title: Jane Bunnett interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 25, 2024

chapter: Advice and becoming a jazz player
title: Advice to young players and mentors Dewey Redman and Don Pullen
summary: She would give her number to a young player, never discourage them, and cites Redman and Pullen as encouraging mentors.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: Yeah. So you’re at a cocktail party and somebody who’s fairly well off gets to know you a little bit. And they say, “So Jane, my niece is a good saxophone player and she wants to be a jazz musician. What do you think about that? What should she do?”

I would say, I would give that person my phone number and say have her call me. That’s exactly what I’d do and that’s what I’ve done. Here’s my phone number. Here’s my email. I’d love to talk to your daughter, niece, whoever it is, and encourage them and then © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

see where they’re coming from. I’ve got a number of young people that call me that are just sort of embarking on maybe, you know, going out there and doing something. But you know unfortunately there’s also a lot of fear of failure and of course everybody — well not everybody because I know people that are fearless, so I’m not fearless. If I’m really, really — what’s the word called — inspired or my vision is so so strong about something I will pursue it. But you know I fear often of failure and I think now that is at just an all-time high and also there’s the other side of that where there’s just plain kind of ignorance and just sort of people that haven’t put the hours in and don’t have the respect for the music in that I feel you should have, and for the history of the music that are out there just glutting the market with terrible stuff. You know really really bad stuff. So there’s a fine line between the two things. I mean it’s just you have to be authentic to yourself and if I see somebody who’s really pursuing something and serious about it I’ll do everything I can. I was — Dewey Redman and Don Pullen they were very big mentors to me and they were probably two of the heaviest musicians sort of out there on the scene. And they were so encouraging to me. So I feel like, you know, if I can try and be like that I should try and do the same thing.
Yeah I’m happy to hear that. Because sometimes the same question another musician would be much more not encouraging. “Well you just better be aware that” this and that.

Yeah I mean I don’t think there’s any point in telling people that because like you know there’s just no reason to discourage somebody. If you don’t make it you don’t make it. You know what I mean? I don’t know, I don’t agree with that. It’s not in my nature to discourage people. They’ll find that out for themself, you know what I mean? You don’t need to tell anybody — and everybody of course develops at such a different pace. I, you know I didn’t pick up my soprano sax until I was, I think I was like thirty — I’m just trying to think how old I was. I was maybe like thirty — what’s the math? I bought my horn in ’78 so what’s the math on that. “88, ’98, so I bought my horn in 1978. I’m 68.
